newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers set to oppose planned cereal aid cuts.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers set to oppose planned cereal aid cuts.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Monday will attack planned cuts in subsidies to cereal and oilseed farmers meant to fund aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis, diplomats said.

Ministers are expected to press for sweeteners for their farmers, which EU farm commissioner Franz Fischler is expected to oppose, and no decision is anticipated until after the European Parliament deliberates in June.
"Ministers will want to get things off their chests," said a Dutch EU Presidency official.
Ministers are expected to argue that the proposed 1.4 billion ecu (1.6 billion dollar) cereal aid cuts are unnecessary, mainly because a firmer dollar has lowered the cost of subsidising exports.
The cereal and oilseed aid cuts were part of an otherwise straightforward 1997/98 (July/June) farm package of mostly unchanged prices proposed last month by Fischler.

The 15 member states at the two-day meeting in Luxembourg will also be briefed on a meat trade dispute with the United States over hygiene rules and discuss olive oil subsidy reforms to curb massive fraud.
Several thousand Italian farmers, angered by EU farm policies, are expected to besiege the milestone 2,000th session of the EU Council of Ministers.
Fischler will brief ministers on new reports on cereals, beef and dairy market trends into the next century which officials say will reinforce the case for more market-oriented reforms.
Diplomats said farm ministers would not change the European Commission's negotiating mandate ahead of a resumption of meat trade talks with the U.S. in Washington next week.
"90 percent has already been agreed. There's only poultry left," the Dutch official said, referring to a row over the U.S.practice of decontaminating chicken carcasses in stagnant chlorinated water.
On April 1, the EU imposed new poultry inspection rules blocking shipments worth an estimated $50 million annually.
Last week, Washington delayed retaliatory measures on some $300 million of imports of EU meat, mainly Danish ham, until April 30 in the hope that agreement could be reached.
On olive oil, Spain is expected to lead producer countries in fiercely attacking a Commission report suggesting that subsidies should be linked to the number of productive trees.
Spain, which says this will result in subsidy cuts throwing tens of thousands of people out of work, wants to simplify the existing aid regime based on production and consumption.
"Both options remain on the table," a Commission spokesman stressed, adding Fischler would visit producer countries to review the situation first hand.
